lesson.title: Beyond Heat: The Universe's Preference for Spreading Out
lesson.summary: Entropy, S, is a thermodynamic quantity that measures how spread out energy and matter are among the ways a system can be arranged, and it is the concept that finally explains which direction processes go, something enthalpy alone cannot do.
lesson.body:
Thermodynamics up to this point has mostly tracked enthalpy: how much heat a process absorbs or releases. But enthalpy alone cannot explain everything you observe. Ice melts spontaneously at room temperature even though melting absorbs heat (an endothermic process that enthalpy alone would seem to disfavor), and a drop of dye spreads through a glass of water even though nothing about energy conservation requires it to. Something besides energy content is steering these processes, and that something is entropy, denoted S. Entropy measures how energy and matter are distributed among the many ways a system's particles could be arranged, and the second law of thermodynamics states that for any spontaneous process, the total entropy of the universe, system plus surroundings, increases. This finally gives chemists a directional principle: processes tend to proceed in whichever direction increases total entropy, even when that means the system itself absorbs energy.

It helps to build early intuition around a simple, common-sense idea before getting formal about it: energy and matter that are spread out over more possibilities are statistically more likely than energy and matter that are squeezed into fewer possibilities, in the same sense that shuffling a deck of cards is far more likely to produce a jumbled order than the original factory order, simply because there are vastly more jumbled arrangements than there are perfectly ordered ones. The formal version of this idea, connecting entropy to literally counting the number of accessible microscopic arrangements, is developed a few chapters ahead, when microstates and the Boltzmann equation are introduced. For now, entropy can be treated as a state function, like enthalpy, with its own units of J/(mol K) or J/K, that increases when a system becomes more spread out, more energetically dispersed, or has more accessible arrangements available to it.

One directly useful, quantitative relationship connects entropy back to enthalpy and temperature for a reversible process happening at constant temperature, such as a phase change occurring exactly at its transition temperature: delta S = delta H / T, where T is in kelvin. At the melting point, a solid and liquid are in equilibrium, meaning the process is reversible in the thermodynamic sense, so this relationship applies cleanly there.

As a worked example, consider the melting of ice at 0 degrees Celsius, 273 K. The molar enthalpy of fusion of water, the heat required to melt one mole of ice, is about 6.01 kJ/mol, or 6010 J/mol. Applying the relationship: delta S(fus) = 6010 J/mol divided by 273 K, which equals about 22.0 J/(mol K). This positive value makes physical sense: melting converts a rigid, more ordered solid into a liquid where molecules have more freedom to move and more ways to arrange their positions and energies, so entropy increases. This particular number, about 22.0 J/(mol K) for the melting of water, will come back in the very next chapter, where it helps explain why water sometimes freezes spontaneously and sometimes does not, depending on temperature.
